heading: Depth can increase training error, and identity shortcuts can help
definition: beyond some depth, plain batch-normalized convolutional networks reach higher training error than shallower ones, even with longer training, while the same networks with identity residual shortcuts do not (ImageNet and CIFAR-10; He et al. 2016). Special initializations can train very deep plain tanh networks without shortcuts (Xiao et al. 2018), and residual networks can train without normalization (Fixup; Zhang, Dauphin & Ma 2019).
summary: Independent studies support plain-network degradation and successful training with special initialization or Fixup in some settings. Broader claims of shortcut protection and reliable Fixup training are contested by reported convergence and replication failures.

suggested_status.reason: C applies to an unrestricted shortcut-protection or reliable-Fixup reading: arXiv:2002.10801#R9 reports residual-network convergence failure, and arXiv:1903.07120#R17 reports a Fixup replication failure using published code and hyperparameters. Narrower components retain independent support: arXiv:2006.16992#R24 qualitatively supports plain-network degradation, and arXiv:2406.01755 supports specially initialized plain tanh training through a verdict without retained rows. counts: versions.V3.verdicts.supports.studies = 5; versions.V3.verdicts.limits_scope.studies = 5; versions.V3.verdicts.challenges.studies = 1; versions.V3.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 0. These results do not establish failure of the original matched shallower comparisons or refute the existential initialization exceptions.
suggested_status.open_questions: A matched independent plain-versus-identity-shortcut depth sweep with final classification errors and extended-training controls would strengthen the core comparison. Repeated Fixup tests under matched published recipes would clarify reliability. Direct independent replication of the dense very-deep tanh setting would distinguish replication from the sparse extension.

source.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
source.authors: Kaiming He; Xiangyu Zhang; Shaoqing Ren; Jian Sun

original_result.setup: He et al. compared plain and identity-shortcut convolutional networks with batch normalization on ImageNet and CIFAR-10.
original_result.result: On ImageNet, the 34-layer plain network had higher training error than the 18-layer plain network throughout training, while the 34-layer ResNet outperformed the 18-layer ResNet and 34-layer plain network. On CIFAR-10, plain-110's error exceeded 60%, while ResNet-1202 achieved below 0.1% training error.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: Fixup converged faster without batch normalization in the 34-layer CIFAR-10 network.
Fixup ResNet-56 and ResNet-110 reached low training losses on CIFAR-10 without normalization.
A plain 101-layer batch-normalized ImageNet network failed to converge.
A spiking network design reduced training loss as depth increased on ImageNet.
Sparse orthogonal initialization enabled 1000-layer tanh MLPs and CNNs to learn without shortcuts.
Fixup failed to converge in 2 of 5 normalization-free ResNet1202 runs.
Deeper CIFAR-10 residual networks trained worse early but could later escape stalled states.
Fixup diverged in 18-layer Transformers trained with half precision and dropout.
As conventional spiking ResNets grew deeper, their training loss rose despite residual shortcuts.
Fixup training failed after four epochs in Res-112 with a 109-layer residual stem.
A 2402-layer CIFAR-10 ResNet failed to converge despite residual connections.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

wording_issues.phrase: while the same networks with identity residual shortcuts do not
wording_issues.issue: Shortcut protection depends on depth and residual-unit design. Early degradation persists in deep CIFAR-10 ResNets, the tested 2402-layer network fails to converge, and conventional spiking residual blocks degrade with depth.

Several extensions measure training loss or convergence rather than classification error. In Identity Mappings, Figure 3 supplies a baseline training-loss curve with no numerical training-classification-error rate; this standalone control cannot establish depth-dependent degradation. The isometric-learning support is qualitative convergence evidence rather than a numerical training-error comparison.

wording_issues.phrase: residual networks can train without normalization
wording_issues.issue: The existential claim has supporting results, but does not establish reliable training across seeds, architectures or numerical settings: Fixup failures occur in ResNet1202, the unusual Res-112 architecture and the tested Transformer transfer.

The original ImageNet rows include a prolonged training procedure, but the independent studies' untested-parts lines leave the matched longer-training control untested. Early loss degradation alone does not establish persistence after longer training.

method_sensitivity.what: Scaled, gated and convolutional shortcuts have worse reported training behavior than identity shortcuts. Normalization after addition impedes training-loss reduction, while pre-activation improves the plotted initial training-loss reduction in ResNet-1001 (Figure 1).

Depth-related loss degradation in CIFAR-10 ResNets is strongest before the first learning-rate reduction; later escape means the outcome depends on when training is assessed. Extreme depth can instead produce convergence failure.
Conventional spiking residual blocks and SEW ADD blocks show opposite depth trends on ImageNet: increasing versus decreasing training loss. The SEW result also includes increasing training accuracy.

arXiv:1806.05393 reports successful training of plain tanh CNNs through 10,000 layers under critical Delta-Orthogonal initialization, with depth-independent learning time; exact training-accuracy endpoints are unstated. arXiv:2406.01755 demonstrates a sparse orthogonal extension for plain tanh networks. In arXiv:1910.02840, CIFAR-10 Fixup training of a 34-layer BasicBlock network requires a small learning rate with unnormalized inputs, while faster convergence remains observed; no Fixup depth or architecture sweep is reported. Separately, arXiv:1903.07120 reports convergence failures for CIFAR-10 ResNet1202 using published Fixup code and hyperparameters.
